About: the radius of a uniform sphere held up by a degenerate gas, found where its total energy is least

About this simulation

On screen
Top: the star drawn to scale as a glowing white disc at the centre of a fixed frame on a dark sky. The frame reaches 15 000 km from the centre for electrons, with the Earth (6371 km) beside the star and a 5000 km scale bar, and 25 km for neutrons, with a 10 km scale bar and a dashed circle at the Schwarzschild radius 2GM/c². Switching the carrier zooms smoothly by a factor of 600. Bottom: the radius against the mass on a logarithmic radius axis, with the Earth's radius and the dashed Schwarzschild line; every mass you visit leaves a point, blue for electrons and a second colour for neutrons.
Controls
The mass slider sets M from 0.20 to 2.00 M☉; the chips and the number box beside it set an exact mass. The carrier chooses degenerate electrons (μe = 2, carbon and oxygen) or degenerate neutrons. Clear points empties the radius–mass plot.
Measured
R is the radius at the minimum of the kinetic energy of the degenerate gas plus the gravitational energy −3GM²/5R, in km and in Earth radii; Rs = 2GM/c²; pF/mc is the Fermi momentum of the carrier in units of its own mass times c. All of these are in the Readouts panel of the sidebar. The disc easing (0.5 s), the collapse (2 s) and the zoom (3 s) are display choices.
Model
A uniform sphere at T = 0; its radius is where kinetic plus gravitational energy is least. Electrons at any speed, neutrons non-relativistic. No nuclear force, no heat, no general relativity. These simplifications matter. The uniform sphere puts the electron limit at 1.72 M☉; a proper polytrope of index 3 gives the Chandrasekhar mass, 1.44 M☉ (1.46 M☉ for μe = 2 exactly). The neutrons here reach pF ≈ 0.55 mnc at 2 M☉, where the non-relativistic energy is already noticeably off, and real neutron stars are shaped by nuclear forces and general relativity, which set a maximum mass near 2.2 M☉.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A heavier white dwarf

Choose degenerate electrons and set the mass to 0.6 M☉. Read the radius. Before moving the slider, predict what happens to the white dwarf when its mass is doubled to 1.2 M☉. Then raise the mass and watch the disc beside the Earth.

2 · Towards two solar masses

Keep degenerate electrons and the mass at 1.2 M☉. Before moving the slider further, predict what the radius does as the mass is raised slowly towards 2.0 M☉. Then raise it in small steps, or type masses into the box, and watch the disc and the points in the R–M plot.

3 · The electrons near the limit

The mass is back at 0.6 M☉, where the electrons' Fermi momentum is about 0.72 mec. Before you raise the mass to 1.71 M☉, predict what happens to the electrons that makes the radius fall towards zero. Then set 1.71 M☉ with the chip or the number box; the Fermi momentum readout returns once you answer.

4 · Held up by neutrons

Set the mass to 1.0 M☉ with degenerate electrons and read the radius. Before switching the carrier, predict the radius of a star of the same mass held up by degenerate neutrons. Then switch to neutrons and watch the zoom.

5 · A heavier neutron star

Keep degenerate neutrons and the mass at 1.0 M☉, and read the ratio of the radius to the Schwarzschild radius. Before moving the slider, predict what happens to this ratio as the mass is raised to 2.0 M☉. Then raise the mass and watch the dashed circle.

6 · What you found

A degenerate star settles where its kinetic plus gravitational energy is least, and a heavier star is a smaller one. With electrons the radius plunges to zero near 1.72 M☉ in this uniform-sphere model, once the electrons become relativistic; the full calculation puts the Chandrasekhar mass at 1.44 M☉. Neutrons, 1840 times heavier, make stars about 400 times smaller, only a few Schwarzschild radii across, where general relativity and nuclear forces, both left out here, take over.

The Physics

The Size of a Compact Star · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A star that has stopped burning is held up by degenerate pressure, and it has a definite size. This sim finds the radius at which a uniform sphere has the least total energy, and draws that star to scale: beside the Earth for electrons, beside its own Schwarzschild radius for neutrons.

What you'll learn

  • Why a degenerate star has one definite radius.
  • What the Fermi momentum pF/mc says about its electrons.
  • How the radius depends on the mass.
  • What changes when neutrons do the holding up.
Both terms in units where C1 = C2 = 1. The star sits where the sum is lowest.

What's on screen

  • Top canvas: the star as a white disc, drawn to scale in a fixed frame. With electrons the frame reaches 15 000 km from the centre, with the Earth beside it and a 5000 km bar. With neutrons the frame changes (its size is printed in the corner), with its own scale bar and a dashed orange circle at Rs = 2GM/c².
  • Bottom canvas: R against M on a log axis, with the Earth's radius and the dashed Rs line. Each mass you visit leaves a point, blue for electrons and violet for neutrons.
  • Readouts: M, R, R/R⊕, Rs, R/Rs and pF/mc.
See itLook at the opening scene. Watch for: a white disc a little larger than the Earth beside it, and one blue point on the plot below.

03

The star settles where the energy is least

A uniform sphere of mass M and radius R holds N = M/(μemH) electrons. Packing them closer raises their kinetic energy, while gravity lowers the total. For slow electrons the notes give (5.10, 5.11):

E = EK + Egrav = C1/R² − C2/R, Egrav = −3GM²/5R

The sum has one minimum, where dE/dR = 0, at R = 2C1/C2. That is the stable star. With N = M/μemH it becomes (5.12):

R = (9π/4)2/3 ħ² / [ G me (μemH)5/3 ] · M−1/3

So M R³ is the same for every white dwarf of this composition. At the minimum 2EK + Egrav = 0, the virial theorem. The formula gives 8481 km for 0.6 M☉, the notes' 8.5 × 10⁶ m, and 7153 km for 1.0 M☉, about 7 × 10⁶ m, close to the radius of Sirius B.

The sim reads 7252 km at 0.6 M☉, because its electrons are not limited to low speeds. Section 04 explains the gap.

Key idea. The radius is not chosen. It is where kinetic plus gravitational energy is least.
See itStart from the opening 0.6 M☉ star, then double the mass. Watch for: the white disc shrinking from 7252 km to 3961 km, smaller than the Earth disc, and a second point on the plot.
04

The Fermi momentum x says how fast the electrons are

Write x = pF/(mec), the readout pF/mc. The Fermi momentum is pF = ħ(9πN/4)1/3/R, so squeezing the star, or adding mass, raises x. The kinetic energy per electron is mec² g(x), the average of √(1+q²) − 1 over the Fermi sphere, and the sim uses this exact g:

g(x) = (3/x³) ∫0x q² (√(1 + q²) − 1) dq
Solid: the exact g(x). Dashed: its two limits, 0.3x² at small x and ¾x − 1 at large x. The curve leaves the parabola near x = 1.

For x ≪ 1, g ≈ 0.3x² and EK goes as 1/R², which is section 03. For x ≫ 1, g ≈ ¾x − 1, so g/x → ¾ and EK → ¾N pFc, which goes as 1/R (5.13).

At 0.6 M☉ the sim has x = 0.725. At 1.2 M☉ it has x = 1.67, and x passes 1 near 0.83 M☉. By then the low-speed formula is wrong: it gives 6732 km at 1.2 M☉, where the sim reads 3961 km.

See itRead the Fermi momentum at 1.2 M☉ with electrons. Watch for: pF/mc reading 1.672, above 1, with R = 3961 km.
05

The radius plunges to zero as the mass nears 1.72 M☉

When the electrons are ultra-relativistic, EK = C3/R with C3 ∝ M4/3 (5.13), the same form as gravity, where C2 ∝ M². The total E = (C3 − C2)/R then has no minimum. If C3 > C2 the star expands. If C3 < C2 the energy falls without limit as R shrinks, and electron pressure cannot stop the collapse. The boundary C3 = C2 is (5.14):

MCh = (15√5π/16) (ħc/G)3/2 / (μemH)²

For μe = 2 this uniform-sphere estimate is 1.72 M☉. In the sim R falls from 7252 km at 0.6 M☉ to 2361 km at 1.5, 450 km at 1.71 (x = 16.6) and 70 km at 1.719. At 1.72 M☉ and above R reads "none (collapse)".

The exact Lane–Emden value in the notes is about 1.4 M☉, so the estimate is a little high.

Electrons, μe = 2. The dashed curve is the low-speed R ∝ M−1/3. Dots: 0.6, 1.2 and 1.71 M☉.
M carrier

See itRaise the mass from 1.2 M☉ in steps towards the limit. Watch for: the disc shrinking to a dot, the plot points diving, and a shaded "collapse" region once R reads "none (collapse)".
See itSet 1.71 M☉ and read the radius. Watch for: R = 450 km and pF/mc = 16.57, with the star a dot beside the Earth.
06

Neutrons make the same minimum about 400 times smaller

With neutrons the particles that give the pressure also give the mass, so me and μemH are both replaced by mn in (5.12). The result is (5.30):

R = (9π/4)2/3 ħ² / (G mn8/3) · M−1/3

For 1.4 M☉ this gives 11 km in the notes, and the sim reads 11.03 km. At 1.0 M☉ it reads 12.33 km, against 4956 km for electrons: 402 times smaller. At low speed alone the ratio would be about 580, which is mn/me = 1839 times (mn/μemH)5/3 ≈ 0.32.

Compare with Rs = 2GM/c², 2.954 km at 1.0 M☉. R/Rs = 4.18 there. Since R ∝ M−1/3 and Rs ∝ M, R/Rs ∝ M−4/3, and it falls to 1.66 at 2.0 M☉.

There pF = 0.55 mnc, so the low-speed energy is already noticeably off. The sim also leaves out nuclear forces and general relativity, which set a real maximum near 2.2 M☉.

Neutrons, low-speed model. R/Rs falls as M−4/3. Dots: 1.0 and 2.0 M☉.
See itSet 1.0 M☉ and switch the carrier to neutrons. Watch for: the frame zooming from 15 000 km to 25 km, a 12.33 km disc about four times the radius of the dashed orange Rs circle, and R/Rs = 4.176.
See itWith neutrons, raise the mass from 1.0 to 2.0 M☉. Watch for: the disc closing in on the orange circle, R/Rs falling to 1.657.
07

Where it matters

  • White dwarfs. A mass of 0.6 M☉ is close to the most common one, and its radius is a little larger than the Earth's. At 1.0 M☉ the low-speed formula gives about 7 × 10⁶ m, close to the radius of Sirius B. Measured white-dwarf masses in binaries are all below about 1.4 M☉.
  • The Chandrasekhar mass does not contain the electron mass, since an ultra-relativistic electron's energy does not depend on it. The sim's 1.72 M☉ is the uniform-sphere estimate, not the exact value.
  • Neutron stars. X-rays from their hot surfaces give radii of 10 to 14 km, and their mean density is a few times 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, like that inside a nucleus.
  • What the sim leaves out: temperature, nuclear forces and general relativity. Its neutron limit is therefore not reliable near 2 M☉.
08

Summary

In one line. A degenerate star settles at the radius where its kinetic plus gravitational energy is least, and the sim draws that radius to scale.

Key points

  • E = C1/R² − C2/R is least at R = 2C1/C2 ∝ M−1/3, while the electrons are slow.
  • x = pF/mc passes 1 near 0.83 M☉, and then R falls faster than M−1/3.
  • With ultra-relativistic electrons E ∝ 1/R has no minimum: the sim's limit is 1.72 M☉ (1.4 M☉ exactly).
  • With neutrons the radius is about 400 times smaller: 12.33 km, R/Rs = 4.18, at 1.0 M☉.

Common mix-ups

  • "R ∝ M−1/3 holds up to the limit." It is a low-speed result: at 1.2 M☉ it gives 6732 km, the sim 3961 km.
  • "1.72 M☉ is Chandrasekhar's mass." It is the uniform-sphere estimate. The exact value is about 1.4 M☉.
  • "A neutron star is a heavier white dwarf." Its carrier is 1839 times heavier, so R is only a few Rs.

Things to try on your own

  • With electrons, find the mass where pF/mc crosses 1.
  • With neutrons, compare R/Rs at 0.6 and 2.0 M☉.
  • Visit several masses, press Clear points, then retrace the plunge.
